title: Program Design
overview: Program design turns a problem into a plan that can be coded. This topic covers two design tools. A structure chart breaks a problem into modules and shows the parameters passed between them. A state-transition diagram documents an algorithm that behaves as a finite state machine. Paper 2 asks candidates to describe the purpose of a structure chart, to complete or draw one for a given problem, to write the pseudocode a chart describes, and to read a state-transition diagram, usually by completing a state-transition table or tracing a sequence of inputs. Answers score when every parameter on a chart is named and points the right way, when each module in the pseudocode becomes a procedure or function whose parameters match the arrows, and when a trace follows the arrows exactly, starting from the start state.
syllabusPoints: Use a structure chart to decompose a problem into sub-tasks and express the parameters passed between the various modules, procedures and functions which are part of the algorithm design.
Describe the purpose of a structure chart.
Construct a structure chart for a given problem.
Derive equivalent pseudocode from a structure chart.
Show understanding of the purpose of state-transition diagrams to document an algorithm.

definitions.definition: A diagram of the modular structure of a solution. Each box is a module, each level refines the level above it, and labelled arrows show the parameters passed between modules.
A self-contained part of a solution that carries out one sub-task. On a structure chart it is a box; in the program it becomes a procedure or a function.
A value passed between modules. On a structure chart a downward arrow supplies a value to the module being called, and an upward arrow returns a value to the calling module.
The parameters that pass between a calling module and the module it calls. A structure chart shows each module's interface as the named arrows on the line joining the two boxes.
A Boolean parameter that reports a condition, such as whether an input was valid. On a structure chart its arrow has a solid (filled) circle at the tail.
A machine with a fixed set of possible states, a start state, a set of inputs that move it from one state to another, and possibly a set of outputs.
A table that gives, for each current state and each input, the next state the FSM moves to and any output it produces.

A diagram that describes the behaviour of an FSM. States are circles and each transition is an arrow labelled with the input that causes it, written input | output when the transition also produces an output.

sections.title: The purpose of a structure chart
content: A structure chart is a design tool for modular programs. The problem is decomposed into sub-tasks, and each sub-task becomes a module drawn as a box. The top box (level 0) names the whole program. The boxes below it (level 1) are the sub-tasks it calls, and any of those can be refined again into its own lower level. This is top-down design with stepwise refinement: each level adds detail to the level above it.

Lines join each module to the modules it calls, and the calls on one level are normally read from left to right. A structure chart shows what the program does and how its modules fit together. It does not show how a module does its job. The detailed logic of each module is written separately in pseudocode or drawn as a flowchart.

A structure chart also shows the interface between modules: the parameters passed each time one module calls another. This lets several programmers each write a module, knowing exactly what data it receives and what it must return, and it shows which modules can be tested or reused on their own.
bullets: Purpose: decompose a problem into sub-tasks (modules), showing the hierarchy of modules and the parameters passed between them.
Each box is a module; each level is a refinement of the level above (top-down design, stepwise refinement).
It shows which module calls which and the interface, not the logic inside a module.
Benefits: helps programmers see how modules are related, lets modules be shared out, written and tested separately, and shows the parameters each module needs.

sections.title: Showing parameters on a structure chart
content: Every parameter is drawn as a short arrow beside the line joining two modules, labelled with the parameter's identifier. The direction of the arrow shows which way the value travels. A downward arrow supplies a value from the calling module to the module it calls. An upward arrow returns a new value from the called module to the module above it. A double-headed arrow shows a value that is passed down, updated inside the lower module, and passed back up.

Two arrow styles are commonly used. A data parameter is often drawn with an open (hollow) circle at its tail. A flag, a Boolean value that reports a condition such as Valid or GameFinished, is drawn with a solid circle at its tail.

A value produced by one module and needed by another is passed up to their common parent and then down again. Modules on the same level never pass values to each other directly. The structure chart does not state whether a parameter is passed by value or by reference; that decision is made when the pseudocode is written.
bullets: Downward arrow: a value supplied to the lower-level (called) module.
Upward arrow: a value returned to the higher-level (calling) module.
Double-headed arrow: a value passed down, changed inside the module, and passed back up.
Solid circle at the tail: a flag (Boolean); open circle: a data value.
Sibling modules exchange data only through their parent; the chart does not say BYVAL or BYREF.

sections.title: Selection and repetition on a structure chart
content: A structure chart can also show control information. Selection is drawn as a diamond on the line below a module, with the condition written beside it. The branches are labelled True and False, and only one of the modules below the diamond is called each time. For example, a CheckLogin module might test PasswordCorrect and call either OutputWelcome (True) or OutputWarning (False).

Repetition is drawn as a semi-circular (curved) arrow across the lines to the modules that are repeated, labelled with the condition that controls the loop, such as UNTIL Valid or WHILE game not finished. Every module under the arrow is called again on each pass.
bullets: Diamond with a condition: selection; one of the True / False branches is called.
Semi-circular arrow with a label: repetition of the modules beneath it; the label gives the loop condition.
In pseudocode a diamond becomes an IF statement and a semi-circular arrow becomes a loop (REPEAT, WHILE or FOR).

examples.label: The CheckLogin diamond written as pseudocode
examples.content:
PROCEDURE CheckLogin(PasswordCorrect : BOOLEAN)
   IF PasswordCorrect = TRUE THEN
      CALL OutputWelcome()
   ELSE
      CALL OutputWarning()
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

sections.title: Constructing a structure chart for a given problem
content: Start with one box naming the whole problem. Split it into the main sub-tasks, usually input, processing and output, and draw them left to right in the order they are carried out. Refine any sub-task that is still too large into a lower level. Then, for each line, decide what data the called module needs (downward arrows) and what it produces for its caller (upward arrows), and name each arrow with a meaningful identifier. Finally, add a diamond for any module that is only called under a condition and a semi-circular arrow for any modules that repeat.
The worked example designs a program that reads a journey distance, repeating the input until it is a positive number, then works out the fuel cost and the travel time and outputs both.
bullets: Top box: the whole problem; level 1: the main sub-tasks in order, left to right.
Refine large sub-tasks into a further level until each box is one clear task.
Add a named arrow for every value a module needs (down) or produces (up).
Add diamonds for conditional calls and semi-circular arrows for repeated calls.

examples.label: Worked example: structure chart for the journey program
examples.content:
Level 0:  JourneyCost

Level 1 (called by JourneyCost, left to right):
  InputDistance      up:   Distance
  CalculateJourney   down: Distance        up: Cost, Hours
  OutputResults      down: Cost, Hours

Level 2 (called by InputDistance, under a semi-circular arrow labelled UNTIL Valid):
  GetNumber          up:   Distance
  CheckPositive      down: Distance        up: Valid  (flag, solid circle)

Reading the interface:
- Distance goes up from InputDistance to JourneyCost, then down into CalculateJourney.
  The two level-1 modules do not pass it to each other directly.
- CalculateJourney returns two values (Cost and Hours), so both arrows point up.
- Valid is a Boolean, so it is drawn as a flag.
- The semi-circular arrow means GetNumber and CheckPositive are called again
  until Valid is TRUE.

sections.title: Deriving pseudocode from a structure chart
content: Each box below the top becomes a subroutine, and the top box becomes the main program that calls the level-1 modules in order. Use local variables and parameters rather than global variables, so each module is self-contained and a change inside one module cannot accidentally alter a variable elsewhere.

The arrows decide the header. A module that sends exactly one value up can be written as a FUNCTION that RETURNS that value. A module that sends no value up is a PROCEDURE called with CALL, with its downward values as BYVAL parameters. A module that sends two or more values up, or has a double-headed arrow, is a PROCEDURE whose upward values are BYREF parameters, so the changes reach the caller. A diamond becomes an IF statement, and a semi-circular arrow becomes a loop whose condition matches the label.
Because the chart does not say how parameters are passed, choose BYVAL for values that only travel down and BYREF for values that must come back up in a procedure.
bullets: Top box: main program; every other box: a procedure or function with the same identifier.
One upward value: FUNCTION ... RETURNS; no upward value: PROCEDURE with BYVAL parameters.
Several upward values or a double-headed arrow: PROCEDURE with BYREF parameters.
Diamond → IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF; semi-circular arrow → REPEAT ... UNTIL, WHILE ... ENDWHILE or FOR ... NEXT.

examples.label: Pseudocode derived from the journey structure chart
examples.content:
CONSTANT CostPerKm = 0.25        // dollars per km
CONSTANT AverageSpeed = 50      // km per hour

FUNCTION GetNumber() RETURNS REAL          // one value up: Distance
   DECLARE Value : REAL
   OUTPUT "Enter the distance in km: "
   INPUT Value
   RETURN Value
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION CheckPositive(Distance : REAL) RETURNS BOOLEAN   // flag up: Valid
   RETURN Distance > 0
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION InputDistance() RETURNS REAL      // one value up: Distance
   DECLARE Distance : REAL
   DECLARE Valid : BOOLEAN
   REPEAT                                  // the semi-circular arrow
      Distance ← GetNumber()
      Valid ← CheckPositive(Distance)
   UNTIL Valid = TRUE
   RETURN Distance
ENDFUNCTION

// two values up, so a procedure with BYREF parameters
PROCEDURE CalculateJourney(BYVAL Distance : REAL, BYREF Cost : REAL, BYREF Hours : REAL)
   Cost ← Distance * CostPerKm
   Hours ← Distance / AverageSpeed
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE OutputResults(Cost : REAL, Hours : REAL)   // values only come down
   OUTPUT "Fuel cost: $", Cost
   OUTPUT "Travel time: ", Hours, " hours"
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program: the JourneyCost box
DECLARE Distance, Cost, Hours : REAL
Distance ← InputDistance()
CALL CalculateJourney(Distance, Cost, Hours)
CALL OutputResults(Cost, Hours)

// Test run: inputs -40 then 120
// -40 fails CheckPositive, so the loop asks again; 120 passes.
// Cost = 120 * 0.25 = 30, Hours = 120 / 50 = 2.4
// Output: Fuel cost: $30   Travel time: 2.4 hours

sections.title: Finite state machines and state-transition tables
content: Some algorithms are best described by the states they can be in rather than by a sequence of steps: a burglar alarm, a door lock or a vending machine. Each can be modelled as a finite state machine (FSM). An FSM has a fixed set of states and one start state. Each input moves it from its current state to a next state, which may be the same state. It may also produce an output.

A state-transition table lists this behaviour. Each row gives a current state, an input (event), the next state and, if there is one, the output. Building the table from a written description is usually the first step, because it forces every combination of state and input to be considered. Any combination the description does not mention shows a gap in the specification that must be resolved.
bullets: FSM: a fixed set of states, a start state, inputs that change the state, and possibly outputs.
An input can leave the FSM in the same state (no change of state).
State-transition table columns: current state, input, (output), next state.
Purpose: documents an algorithm precisely, including what each input does in every state, before it is coded.

examples.label: Worked example: state-transition table for a code-operated locker
examples.content:
Description: A locker starts Locked. Entering the correct code unlocks it. One wrong
code gives a Warning; a correct code from Warning still unlocks it, but a second wrong
code Blocks the locker until a member of staff resets it. Closing the door of an
unlocked locker locks it again.

Current state | Input         | Next state
--------------+---------------+-----------
Locked        | Correct code  | Unlocked
Locked        | Wrong code    | Warning
Warning       | Correct code  | Unlocked
Warning       | Wrong code    | Blocked
Unlocked      | Door closed   | Locked
Blocked       | Staff reset   | Locked

Trace the input sequence: Wrong, Correct, Door closed, Wrong, Wrong
Locked -> Warning -> Unlocked -> Locked -> Warning -> Blocked

Note: the FSM counts wrong attempts by being in a different state (Warning),
not by using a variable. The description does not say what a code does while
Blocked; a designer would add a row such as Blocked | any code | Blocked.

sections.title: Drawing and reading state-transition diagrams
content: A state-transition diagram shows the same information as the table. Each state is a circle labelled with its name. The start state has an arrow pointing into it from nowhere, often labelled start. Each transition is an arrow from the current state to the next state, labelled with the input that causes it. An input that causes no change of state is drawn as an arrow that loops back to the same circle. A final (halting) state, if the FSM has one, is drawn as a double circle.

When a transition also produces an output, the arrow's label is written input | output. For example, 1 | 0 means an input of 1 produces an output of 0 as the FSM follows that arrow. An FSM with outputs is also called a Mealy machine. If there is no output for a transition, exam tables often write none in the output column.

To trace an input sequence, start in the start state. For each input, find the arrow leaving the current state that carries that input, record the output on its label, and move to the state it points to. The next input is always taken from this new state.
bullets: Circle: a state; double circle: a final (halting) state; arrow from nowhere into a state: the start state.
Arrow labelled with an input: a transition; a loop back to the same circle: no change of state.
Label input | output: the output produced by that transition (Mealy machine).
Tracing: always begin in the start state, and take each new input from the state reached by the previous one.

examples.label: Worked example: tracing an FSM with outputs
examples.content:
An FSM reads a bit stream one bit at a time and outputs 1 whenever the bit just read
is the second (or later) of consecutive 1s; otherwise it outputs 0.
Start state: S1 (the last bit was 0, or nothing has been read yet).

Transitions (diagram labels):
  S1 --0|0--> S1   (loop back to S1)
  S1 --1|0--> S2
  S2 --1|1--> S2   (loop back to S2)
  S2 --0|0--> S1

Trace for the input 0 1 1 1 0 1 1:
Current state | Input | Output | Next state
S1            | 0     | 0      | S1
S1            | 1     | 0      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2
S2            | 0     | 0      | S1
S1            | 1     | 0      | S2
S2            | 1     | 1      | S2

Output stream: 0 0 1 1 0 0 1   Final state: S2

Each row's current state is the previous row's next state.

diagram.title: Reading a structure chart from the top down
nodes: Level 0: one box naming the whole problem (becomes the main program)
Level 1: the main sub-tasks, called left to right (input, processing, output)
Level 2 and below: each sub-task refined into smaller modules (stepwise refinement)
Arrows on each line: parameters down to the called module, results up to the caller; solid circle = flag
Control: a diamond for selection, a semi-circular arrow for repetition

analysisChains.title: Choosing the header for a module from its arrows
steps: A structure chart shows a module ProcessOrder with downward arrows Quantity and UnitPrice and upward arrows Total and Discount
Two values travel up, and a function can return only one value
So ProcessOrder must be a procedure, and Total and Discount must be passed by reference so the caller receives the new values
Quantity and UnitPrice only travel down, so they can be passed by value
analysisChains.evaluation: The header is PROCEDURE ProcessOrder(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER, BYVAL UnitPrice : REAL, BYREF Total : REAL, BYREF Discount : REAL). Writing it as a FUNCTION, or passing Total BYVAL, would lose at least one of the results the chart says must be returned.

analysisChains.title: A module that uses a value its chart never passes to it
steps: In a chart for a quiz program, CheckAnswer has a downward arrow Answer and an upward flag Correct
The pseudocode for CheckAnswer compares Answer with the variable RightAnswer
No arrow carries RightAnswer into CheckAnswer, so the module can only reach it as a global variable
A global variable means CheckAnswer is no longer self-contained: it cannot be tested on its own, and a change to RightAnswer elsewhere affects it without appearing in its interface
analysisChains.evaluation: Add a downward arrow RightAnswer to the chart and a matching parameter to the header, so the interface on the chart and the parameters in the code agree. Every value a module uses from outside should appear as an arrow on its line.

analysisChains.title: Finding a gap when turning a description into an FSM
steps: A description of a turnstile says: in Locked, a coin unlocks it; in Unlocked, a push lets one person through and locks it
Building the state-transition table row by row for every state and every input gives four combinations
Two combinations are not described: a push while Locked, and a coin while Unlocked
Without rows for them the diagram has states with no arrow for an input, so the algorithm's behaviour for that input is undefined
analysisChains.evaluation: The designer adds Locked | push | Locked and Unlocked | coin | Unlocked (loops back to the same state, perhaps with an output such as returning the coin). This is the purpose of the table and diagram: they document every state and input, so gaps are found and settled before coding.

examTips: When asked for the purpose of a structure chart, give both parts: it shows the decomposition into modules (the hierarchy / which module calls which) and the parameters passed between them (the interface).
Label every arrow with the parameter's identifier and check its direction: down for a value the module needs, up for a value it produces.
When writing pseudocode from a chart, keep the module identifiers and parameter names from the chart, and make the number of parameters in each header match the number of arrows.
In a state-transition trace, the current state of each row is the next state of the row before; write none in the output column when a transition produces no output.
Read an input | output label from left to right: the input causes the transition and the output is produced as the FSM moves.
commonMistakes: Drawing a structure chart with the logic inside a module (steps, loops of statements) instead of only the modules, calls and parameters.
Drawing an arrow between two modules on the same level instead of passing the value up to the parent and back down.
Writing a module with two upward arrows as a function, or passing its upward values BYVAL so the results never reach the caller.
Forgetting the flag symbol: a Boolean result such as Valid should have a solid circle.
Starting an FSM trace from the wrong state, or taking the next input from the old state instead of the state just reached.
Leaving out transitions that return to the same state, so the table or diagram does not cover every input in every state.

quickRecall.question: State two purposes of a structure chart.
quickRecall.answer: It shows how a problem is decomposed into modules and which module calls which, and it shows the parameters passed between modules (the interface).

quickRecall.question: What does a downward arrow on a structure chart show, and what does an upward arrow show?
quickRecall.answer: A downward arrow is a value supplied to the called (lower) module; an upward arrow is a value returned to the calling (higher) module.

quickRecall.question: How is a flag shown on a structure chart?
quickRecall.answer: As an arrow with a solid (filled) circle at its tail; it carries a Boolean value.

quickRecall.question: How are selection and repetition shown on a structure chart?
quickRecall.answer: Selection by a diamond with a condition and True / False branches; repetition by a semi-circular arrow labelled with the loop condition.

quickRecall.question: A module on a chart returns one value upward. How is it usually written in pseudocode?
quickRecall.answer: As a FUNCTION with RETURNS, taking its downward values as parameters.

quickRecall.question: What does a structure chart not tell you about parameters?
quickRecall.answer: Whether they are passed by value or by reference; that is decided when the pseudocode is written.

quickRecall.question: What is a finite state machine?
quickRecall.answer: A machine with a fixed set of states, a start state, inputs that change it from one state to another, and possibly outputs.

quickRecall.question: What does the label b | c on a state-transition diagram mean?
quickRecall.answer: An input of b causes this transition and produces an output of c.

quickRecall.question: How are the start state and a final (halting) state shown on a state-transition diagram?
quickRecall.answer: The start state has an arrow pointing into it from nowhere; a final state is drawn as a double circle.
